extracted.intended_audience: researchers, funders, policy-makers and scholars interested in the evidence and design of grant-peer-review systems
extracted.subtask_description: A non-systematic review evaluating what is known about the reliability, biases, predictive validity, and potential reforms of peer review used to allocate research grants. Focuses on empirical evidence (or lack thereof) and proposed procedural changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter-rater reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Inter-rater reliability is consistently low across funding agencies; two reviewers often disagree more than chance would predict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure and report agreement statistics; beware of decisions based on single or only two reviewers. Low agreement implies that acceptance/rejection may be heavily influenced by which reviewers are assigned. Anti-patterns include using very few reviewers and treating single reviewer scores as definitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variability in scoring norms / calibration
rubrics_metrics.description: There is variability in scoring norms across reviewers and panels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement calibration procedures or normalized scoring to reduce between-reviewer and between-panel variability. Without calibration, scores reflect differing reviewer norms rather than proposal quality. Guidance includes use of anchor examples, panel calibration meetings, or statistical normalization of scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Reliance on a small number of reviewers (e.g., two) contributes to low reliability and noisy funding decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple independent reviewers where feasible to improve reliability; consider trade-offs between cost/time and reliability. Anti-pattern: making funding decisions based on very few reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant age can bias review outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor and control for age effects; anonymize where possible or adjust evaluation criteria to reduce differential treatment by age. Anti-patterns include assuming meritocratic neutrality without testing for age-related effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional prestige (Matthew) bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutional prestige influences reviewer judgments ('Matthew effect'), advantaging applicants from well-known institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider anonymization of institutional identifiers, blind review, or statistical adjustment; track outcomes by institution to detect differential treatment. Anti-pattern: allowing institutional affiliation to be a proxy for quality without verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cronyism / personal connections
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal connections and cronyism can distort peer review decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement conflict-of-interest policies, careful reviewer selection, and monitoring for patterns indicative of favoritism. Anti-patterns include weak COI enforcement or allowing reviewers with close ties to applicants to decide on those applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disciplinary / interdisciplinary bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Interdisciplinary work is disadvantaged by peer review structured around disciplinary norms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design panels and reviewer pools to include interdisciplinary expertise; adopt evaluation criteria that recognize integrative approaches. Anti-pattern: evaluating interdisciplinary proposals strictly by single-discipline standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Gender can affect review outcomes (descriptive evidence noted at the Swedish Medical Research Council; findings are mixed elsewhere).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect and analyze gender-disaggregated outcomes; consider anonymization or reviewer training to mitigate implicit bias. Anti-patterns: ignoring gender effects or failing to monitor for disparate outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservatism vs innovation bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review tends to be conservative; innovative proposals often receive lower scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create explicit criteria that reward novelty and high-risk/high-reward work, or allocate specific funds for innovative research. Anti-patterns: favoring safe incremental proposals because reviewers penalize perceived risk or novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictive validity of grant scores
rubrics_metrics.description: Grant scores have weak predictive validity for downstream productivity (e.g., citations, impact); comparative studies assessing effects of peer review procedures on research quality are scarce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require validation studies linking selection decisions to later research outcomes; be cautious about over-interpreting score differences as meaningful indicators of future impact. Anti-patterns: assuming high scores robustly predict future productivity without empirical validation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence-based validation of review procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Conventional wisdom that peer review is the gold standard is largely based on faith rather than evidence; there is a need for systematic empirical studies of peer-review processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fund and incorporate experimental and observational studies that evaluate how different peer-review designs affect funded research quality. Policy changes should be guided by measured outcomes rather than tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-registration of evaluation criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-registration of evaluation criteria is proposed to increase transparency and reduce retrospective flexibility in judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish scoring rubrics and decision rules in advance of review rounds to reduce opportunistic criterion shifting. Anti-patterns: changing implicit criteria mid-competition or failing to make expectations explicit to applicants and reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structured rubrics vs holistic scoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Structured rubrics are recommended over holistic scoring to improve consistency and clarify what is being assessed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt itemized criteria with definitions and anchors rather than single global scores. Use rubrics to make expectations explicit, which facilitates calibration and research on predictive validity. Anti-patterns: relying solely on unstructured, free-form judgments that are hard to compare or study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calibration training for reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Calibration training for reviewers is suggested to reduce variability and improve agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide training sessions, exemplar-rated proposals, and feedback to reviewers before scoring. Monitor whether training improves inter-rater reliability; avoid assuming reviewers share common scoring interpretations without training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity of reviewers / anonymized review
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of multiple anonymous reviewers is suggested to reduce bias and influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ blinded review of applicant identity where feasible, and ensure reviewer anonymity to limit social or reputational influences. Combine anonymity with other safeguards (e.g., COI rules). Anti-patterns: open-review processes without protections against reputational or social pressures when bias is likely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative allocation mechanisms: modified lottery
rubrics_metrics.description: Modified lotteries above a quality threshold are proposed as an alternative to deterministic ranking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement a thresholding step to remove clearly weak proposals, then allocate funding among remaining qualified proposals by lottery to reduce the impact of low reliability and reviewer idiosyncrasy. Consider fairness, legal, and stakeholder acceptability issues when adopting lotteries.
